title: Virtual Memory and Paging
notes: Diagram-heavy: an address split and a page-table lookup drawn in ASCII. The numbers in the worked example must survive (4 KB pages, 12-bit offset). Traps: TLB internals and multi-level tables, which are the natural next topic but are not in this lecture.

pages.text:
Week 5 — Virtual Memory.

Each process sees its own virtual address space. Memory is divided into fixed-size pages (virtual) and frames (physical). With 4 KB pages the low 12 bits of an address are the offset within the page and the remaining high bits are the page number.

  virtual address = | page number | offset (12 bits) |

A page table maps each page number to a frame number. Translation: look up the page number, take the frame number, append the unchanged offset.

  page number --> [page table] --> frame number | offset

Each page table entry also holds a valid bit. If the valid bit is 0 the page is not in memory and the access raises a page fault.

On a page fault the operating system loads the page from disk, updates the page table and restarts the instruction. A page fault costs millions of cycles compared with a memory access, so a high fault rate (thrashing) makes the system crawl.

When no frame is free a page replacement policy chooses a victim. FIFO evicts the oldest page; LRU evicts the least recently used.

required_facts.fact: translation appends the unchanged offset to the frame number
fault handling: load from disk, update table, restart
FIFO evicts the oldest page, LRU the least recently used
